messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] "jumpy" stan trace
parts:
What do you mean by a "jumpy trace"? If you're
using RStan, what does the pairs() plot look like?

Can it fit simulated data? Often Poisson has a problem
because the underlying data is overdispersed (even though
you have a predictor mu here). So it could just be
that the model doesn't fit the data well.

The model is also only weakly identified by priors (and
by pinning B[1] == 0).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] "jumpy" stan trace
parts:
You can't tell from just looking at the traceplots.
If the R-hat values are all near 1 and you have enough
samples as measured by n_eff you should be good to go.

Some of the problem you might be having is that sigma
values near zero can be unstable numerically and
computationally. We use a log transform, which makes
values near 0 very large negative values in the space
in which we actually sample.

If that wasn't an earlier quiery from you, I just
went over how to fit a regression on variance using
the negative binomial.

- Bob

Thanks Bob for leading me through NB parametrizations. Attached is the
model I came up with. This is so called fixed effects gravity model
widely used in economics to model trade flow. Poisson pseudo max
likelihood (PPML) is widely used to estimate model parameters and I
thought I could beat PPML with a model in stan which uses true
likelihood. It looks that stan model is slightly better but not
drastically. Aattached is the trace and model predictions. PPML
predictions are in red. Black circles are median of predictive posterior
vs. observed. Any ideas how to improve the model further? By the way,
all NB parametrizations (mu+mu^2/phi in nb1s.stan or
alpha+beta*mu+gamma*mu^2 in nb1sss.stan or mu=exp(x*theta+eps[i] in
nb1ss.stan) where x is input vector, theta is a vector of coefficients
to estimate and eps[i] is to add extra variation to NB) exhibit similar
trends. Maybe some different distribution will fit/predict better?
Since I have few zeros in the data set lognormal isn't working.

Thank you,
Linas

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] "jumpy" stan trace
parts:
What does alpha in the traceplots correspond to in the
model? If it's A, the prior is very misspecified
because the posterior is in the range of 10e6 and
the prior is normal(0,5).

That's also a very wide prior on elascticity, which
fits very close to 0.9 and gets a cauchy (0, 2.5) prior.
This is less worrying than the prior for A.

Otherwise, I don't really know enough about these models
and don't have enough time to dive in deeply. I do know
that time series models can be hard to fit in terms of
n_eff per iteration, so I wouldn't worry too much about
the relatively poor mixing of elasticity.

If you repost to the list with a subject of the kind of
model you want help with rather than the current subject,
someone else may be able to help.

- Bob
